title: Wi-Fi Photo Frames Family Can Send Pictures To: Aura Carver vs. Nixplay
subtitle: A plain-English look at two connected photo frames, what they cost up front and over time, and what they can and cannot do.
excerpt: A Wi-Fi photo frame lets the grandkids' latest pictures show up on a side table without anyone mailing a print. Here is how the Aura Carver and Nixplay Modern compare, including the subscription question.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Family photos used to arrive in envelopes. Now they live on phones, and plenty of grandparents never see most of them. The pictures are taken, shared in a group text, and then disappear into someone else's camera roll.

A Wi-Fi digital photo frame is one gentle fix. It sits on a shelf or side table and plays a running slideshow. Family can add new pictures from wherever they are, and the frame shows them. Someone with a smartphone does need to handle the setup, which we cover below.

The frame connects to the home's Wi-Fi, the wireless internet signal from the router. With Aura, family and friends can add photos from anywhere or text them to the frame, and Aura's FAQ says the frame needs Wi-Fi to get new content from the cloud, which just means the company's online computers. Nixplay says to download its app, plug in the frame and follow the on-screen guide.
The big difference between brands is cost over time. Aura frames have no subscription fees. Nixplay has a free tier with limits, plus optional yearly plans for more storage and longer video clips.

It helps to be clear about what a frame is not. It only shows photos and short videos. It is not a video-call device, not a two-way speaker, and not a way to check on someone's safety or health. If the home Wi-Fi goes down, new photos stop arriving until it comes back.

items: Ongoing fees: Add any yearly plan to the price of the frame before comparing. Nixplay's paid plans are $19.99 or $29.99 a year; Aura says it has no subscription fees.
Free-tier limits: Nixplay's free tier has 500 MB of photo storage, 15-second video clips, up to 5 frames and 1 shared album. Compare those limits with how many relatives will be sending photos.
Screen size: A 10-inch frame suits a side table or nightstand. Larger frames are easier to see across a room but cost more.
Controls: Aura uses a touch bar and Nixplay a touchscreen. Touch controls may be fiddly for stiff fingers. We have not tried them, so look at one in a store or read reviews if that is a concern.
Wi-Fi type: Aura says its frame needs a 2.4GHz router. We did not check Nixplay's requirement, so confirm it with the maker. Check the router if you are unsure.
Gifting help: Both makers let you preload photos before the frame is given, so it starts out full of pictures.
Privacy: Photos go to the maker's cloud. Nixplay states its storage is USA-based and CCPA and GDPR compliant. We did not check Aura's privacy terms, so read them before setting one up for a parent.

sections.content: Setting it up and keeping it fresh
In most families, an adult child handles the first setup. Aura is direct about the app in its product page FAQ, which means someone with a smartphone has to do the setup:
"Yes, the Aura app is required for setup, inviting loved ones, and adjusting your frame's settings." (Aura, Carver product page FAQ)

Nixplay describes its setup as downloading the app, plugging in the frame and following an on-screen guide. Either way, it is easiest to do this before the frame is wrapped, or during a visit, so the person receiving it only has to plug it in.

The real secret is people, not technology. A frame that never gets new photos turns into a slideshow of the same old pictures. Invite several relatives, and maybe agree that each one adds a few photos a week. Aura also lets family text photos to the frame, which can be handy for less app-minded relatives.

Both frames have features that save fuss. The Aura Carver adjusts its brightness automatically and shuts off in the dark. Nixplay lists an energy-saving smart sensor. As general advice, pick a spot near an outlet and within reach of the Wi-Fi.

Aura's price moves with sales and retailers: the Carver showed a $10 sale in November 2026, and Aura sells a separate model through Costco. Nixplay's price differed between its own pages. Check the live price and the return policy before you buy, and count any yearly plan as part of the real cost.
sections.label: Before You Buy

sections.content: A connected photo frame will not replace a phone call or a visit, but it can bring a steady trickle of everyday moments into a parent's or grandparent's home. Choose the one whose costs and controls fit, set it up together, and keep the pictures coming.

products.name: Aura Carver 10" HD Frame (Charcoal)
products.price: $139 (sale price, November 2026; list price $149); check current price
products.blurb: Suits families who want no ongoing fees: the 10.1-inch frame has no subscription and unlimited photo and video storage through the Aura app, iCloud or Google Photos. Relatives can add photos from anywhere or text them to the frame, and it plays short videos up to 30 seconds with sound.

products.name: Nixplay Modern 10.1" HD Touch Screen
products.price: Check current price: Nixplay's pages disagree, showing $199.99 on the product page and $139.99 (marked down from $199.99) on the collection page
products.blurb: Suits families who like a touchscreen and are curious about Alexa or Google Home, which it works with; syncing from Google Photos, Instagram, Dropbox, Facebook and Alexa is a paid feature, and this is not a monitored alert device. The free tier has 500 MB, 15-second clips, 5 frames and 1 shared album, with optional plans at $19.99 or $29.99 a year.
